name: Kingdom of Strathclyde

imageInfo.caption: Dumbarton Rock from the south-east in a 2016 photograph: the volcanic plug that carried Alt Clut, citadel of the kings of the Clyde. The walls on the summit are eighteenth-century military work.
imageInfo.creator: Rosser1954
imageInfo.note: The rock, not the buildings, is the medieval evidence. It is a twin-peaked volcanic plug 73 metres high at the junction of the Leven and the Clyde, and it carried the fortress the early sources call Alt Clut from at least the fifth century until the Dublin Norse took it in 870. Almost nothing of the early medieval citadel stands above ground: the fourteenth-century portcullis arch is the oldest masonry on the site, and the visible ramparts and batteries are Georgian. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

armsImageInfo.caption: The kingdom bore no coat of arms; its emblem is the carving of its royal church — the five hogback grave-covers at Govan Old, photographed in 2019.
armsImageInfo.creator: Viking870
armsImageInfo.date: 2019; the hogbacks are of the tenth century
armsImageInfo.note: Carved stone, not heraldry: no kingdom in tenth-century Britain bore arms, Strathclyde struck no coin and left no seal, and the Govan monuments are the nearest thing it had to an emblem of its own. These five hogbacks are the largest group of the type in Britain; their house-shaped roofs and gripping end-beasts are Scandinavian in taste, carved for a Brittonic elite at the royal church the kingdom used after Dumbarton Rock fell. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary: The Brittonic kingdom of the Clyde, ruled from the fortress of Alt Clut on Dumbarton Rock until the Dublin Norse destroyed it in 870, and from Govan thereafter, until it was absorbed into Alba in the eleventh century.
overview: The Kingdom of Strathclyde was the last of the northern British kingdoms, a Cumbric-speaking realm on the Clyde whose kings ruled from Dumbarton Rock and, after 870, from Govan. It is the only Brittonic kingdom outside Wales to survive into the eleventh century.
knownFor: Alt Clut, the citadel on Dumbarton Rock
The four-month Viking siege that destroyed the fortress in 870
Govan Old, its royal church, and the carved stones kept there
Cumbric, the last Brittonic speech of northern Britain
Owain the Bald, its last recorded king, who fought at Carham in 1018

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Kingdom of Strathclyde was a Brittonic realm on the river Clyde whose people spoke Cumbric, a language close to Old Welsh. Its earlier name was Alt Clut, the Rock of the Clyde, after the fortress its kings held on Dumbarton Rock; Welsh sources call the later kingdom Ystrad Clud, and English writers called its rulers kings of the Cumbrians rather than kings of Strathclyde.

Its recorded history runs from the fifth century, when Ceretic of Alt Clut received an angry letter from Saint Patrick about slave-taking, to the eleventh, when the last king anyone names fought on the Tweed. At its greatest reach in the tenth century its authority ran from Loch Lomond in the north to the river Eamont near Penrith, deep into what is now Cumbria. No chronicle was written inside it and no archive of its own survives, so the kingdom is visible only through the records of its neighbours.

contentSections.title: Alt Clut, the rock of the Clyde
paragraphs: Dumbarton Rock is a twin-peaked volcanic plug seventy-three metres high, standing where the river Leven joins the Clyde, and for four centuries it was the citadel of the Britons of the north. It commands the estuary in both directions and can be approached from one side only. The kingdom took its name from the fortress rather than from any province, which is a fair description of how it worked: a rock, a royal household, and whatever tribute the household could reach.

Ceretic Guletic, addressed by Saint Patrick, is the earliest king whose name is secure. Rhydderch Hael ruled in the late sixth century and is remembered both in Welsh tradition and in Adomnán's life of Columba, and the church of Glasgow later claimed Saint Kentigern as its founder in his reign. In 642 Eugein son of Beli defeated the Dál Riata and killed their king Domnall Brecc at Strathcarron. A century later the kingdom was under heavy pressure from the east: in 756 a joint Pictish and Northumbrian army forced its king Dumnagual to submit, and in 780 the annals record simply that Alt Clut was burned.

contentSections.title: The fall of Dumbarton, 870
paragraphs: In 870 the Dublin Norse kings Amlaíb and Ímar brought a fleet up the Clyde and laid siege to Dumbarton Rock. The Annals of Ulster record that the attack lasted four months and that the fortress fell when its water failed; Alan Macquarrie's reconstruction has the Norse taking the lower rock, where the well lay, and leaving the defenders penned on the summit without it. Four months is an extraordinary length for Viking warfare in Britain, and it measures how strong the site was rather than how weak.

The following year the annals record the victors returning to Dublin with two hundred ships and a great host of British, English and Pictish captives, bound for what was then among the largest slave markets in Europe. The king, Arthgal, either escaped into Pictland or was taken with them. He was killed in 872, and the annals say it was done at the instigation of Causantín mac Cináeda, king of the Picts — the first clear sign of the pressure from the north-east that would eventually end the kingdom altogether.

contentSections.title: Govan and the new kingdom
paragraphs: The kingdom survived the loss of its fortress but not its old shape. Power moved about twelve miles up-river to Govan, on the south bank of the Clyde opposite Partick, and from 872 the annals stop writing of Alt Clut and start writing of Strathclyde — a realm named for its valley instead of its rock.

Govan Old became the royal church, and its carved stones are the best physical evidence the kingdom left. Thirty-one monuments of the ninth to eleventh centuries survive there: a sandstone sarcophagus, the only one of its kind from pre-Norman northern Britain, carved with a horseman chasing a stag in a Pictish manner; five hogback grave-covers, the largest such group in Britain; four upright crosses, among them the Sun Stone and the Jordanhill Cross; and twenty-one recumbent cross-slabs. Most scholars date the sarcophagus to the ninth century and connect it with the cult of Saint Constantine, to whom the church was dedicated. Fourteen further stones were lost when the neighbouring shipyard was demolished in 1973.

contentSections.title: Between Alba, Northumbria and the Norse
paragraphs: Strathclyde conducted its politics between powers that were all larger than it: Alba to the north-east, the Northumbrians and behind them the kings of Wessex to the south-east, and the Norse-Gaelic world of Dublin and the Isles to the west. Its kings appear in the English record as clients and as enemies by turns, and often as both within a decade.

A king of the Cumbrians was among those who settled with Æthelstan at Eamont in 927, and Owain ap Dyfnwal attested Æthelstan's charters as a sub-king in 931 and 935. In 937 the same king joined Constantine of Alba and Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin in the invasion that Æthelstan destroyed at the Battle of Brunanburh. In 945 Edmund of England ravaged the kingdom; Roger of Wendover, writing nearly three centuries later, adds that he blinded two sons of Dyfnwal and made the kingdom over to Malcolm I of Alba in return for military support. Whatever was agreed did not stick: Dyfnwal ab Owain ruled on, gave up the kingship in old age and died on pilgrimage to Rome in 975.

contentSections.title: Major rulers
paragraphs: Ceretic Guletic (fifth century), the first king whose name survives, known because Saint Patrick wrote to rebuke him for selling Christian captives. Rhydderch Hael (late sixth century), the king of Welsh tradition and of Adomnán's Columba. Eugein son of Beli (mid seventh century), who killed Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata at Strathcarron in 642. Dumnagual (mid eighth century), forced to submit to a joint Pictish and Northumbrian army in 756.

Arthgal (died 872), the last king of Alt Clut, who lost Dumbarton Rock after a four-month siege and was killed two years later at Causantín's prompting. Rhun ab Arthgal, his son, whose marriage into the Alpínid house of Alba began the entanglement with the Scots that outlasted the kingdom. Owain ap Dyfnwal (active in the 920s and 930s), sub-king to Æthelstan and one of the defeated at Brunanburh. Dyfnwal ab Owain (died 975), who ended his life in Rome. Owain the Bald (active 1018), the last king of the Clyde Britons whose name is recorded.

contentSections.title: Owain the Bald and Carham, 1018
paragraphs: The last recorded act of the kingdom was a victory. The Historia Regum attributed to Symeon of Durham says that a great host of Scots under Malcolm II of Scotland, together with Eugenius Calvus — Owain the Bald — king of the Clyde folk, destroyed the Northumbrian army between the Tees and the Tweed. A comet is placed thirty days before the fighting, which fits the astronomical record for August 1018, and Ealdhun, the first bishop of Durham, is said to have died of grief when the news reached him.

The Battle of Carham matters here less for what it settled than for what it shows. The Durham writer gives Owain a royal title of his own, rex Clutinensium, rather than folding him into the Scottish king's following: a century and a half after Dumbarton fell, the kingdom could still put its own army the length of the Tweed valley and fight as a partner rather than a levy. Whether Owain died in the battle is stated nowhere, and the year itself is argued over, because the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle places the death of Uhtred of Bamburgh, whom the Historia names as the beaten commander, in 1016.

contentSections.title: The end of the kingdom
paragraphs: After 1018 the record stops naming kings of the Clyde. There is no account of a conquest, no treaty, no submission and no last stand; a Cumbrian king appears at an English royal assembly about 1031, and then nothing. The usual conclusion is that Alba absorbed the kingdom in the years after Carham, most probably under Malcolm II of Scotland, who reigned until 1034.

That conclusion is less secure than its popularity suggests. A. A. M. Duncan argued that no firm evidence places Strathclyde under the Scots before the time of Malcolm III, two generations later, and in 1054 an English expedition under Earl Siward installed a man the sources call Máel Coluim, son of the king of the Cumbrians — which implies a Cumbrian kingship still existed to be claimed. What is certain is the outcome: by 1107 Alexander I could grant the old kingdom to his brother David as an appanage, and the Clyde had become a Scottish province with a bishopric at Glasgow rather than a realm with a king.

contentSections.title: Why the sources are so thin
paragraphs: No native chronicle, charter, king-list or coin survives from Strathclyde. The kingdom is known through four sets of outsiders' records, each looking at something else. Irish annals, above all the Annals of Ulster, notice it when a Dublin fleet or an Alban king touches it. Welsh material keeps its rulers as distant kinsmen in a shared Brittonic past. English writers, from Bede to the Durham compilers, notice it when it submits to them or beats them. Norse tradition barely notices it at all.

The result is a realm with a five-hundred-year history and about twenty securely known names, most of them attached to a single event apiece. Cumbric died without leaving a literature, so there is no voice from inside the kingdom in any form. What it left instead is on the ground: the Brittonic place-names running from Glasgow through Lanarkshire and into Cumbria, and the carved stones at Govan, which are the only documents the kingdom produced that can still be read.

timeline.title: Saint Patrick writes to Ceretic
timeline.description: Patrick rebukes Ceretic of Alt Clut for seizing and selling Christian captives, the earliest secure notice of the kingdom.

timeline.title: Domnall Brecc killed at Strathcarron
timeline.description: Eugein son of Beli defeats the Dál Riata and kills their king, the high point of Alt Clut power in the seventh century.

timeline.title: Submission to Picts and Northumbrians
timeline.description: A joint army forces King Dumnagual to terms, and Alt Clut is burned again in 780.

timeline.title: Dumbarton Rock falls
timeline.description: Amlaíb and Ímar of Dublin besiege the fortress for four months and take it when the water supply fails.

timeline.title: The captives taken to Dublin
timeline.description: The Annals of Ulster record two hundred ships carrying British, English and Pictish prisoners to the Dublin slave market.

timeline.title: Death of Arthgal
timeline.description: The last king of Alt Clut is killed, the annals say at the instigation of Causantín mac Cináeda of the Picts.

timeline.title: Settlement with Æthelstan at Eamont
timeline.description: A king of the Cumbrians comes to terms with the English king, and attests his charters as a sub-king in 931 and 935.

timeline.title: Brunanburh
timeline.description: Owain ap Dyfnwal joins Constantine of Alba and Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin, and is beaten at the Battle of Brunanburh.

timeline.title: Edmund ravages the kingdom
timeline.description: The English king lays it waste and, by Roger of Wendover's much later account, grants it to Malcolm I of Alba.

timeline.title: Dyfnwal ab Owain dies at Rome
timeline.description: The king gives up his throne in old age and dies on pilgrimage, an unusually well-recorded end for a Cumbrian ruler.

timeline.title: Carham
timeline.description: Owain the Bald fights beside Malcolm II of Scotland and destroys the Northumbrian army between the Tees and the Tweed.

timeline.title: The last Cumbrian king on record
timeline.description: A king of the Cumbrians appears at an English royal assembly, and no ruler of the kingdom is named afterwards.

timeline.title: Siward installs a Cumbrian claimant
timeline.description: An English expedition sets up a Máel Coluim described as son of the king of the Cumbrians, implying the kingship still existed.

timeline.title: Granted to David as an appanage
timeline.description: Alexander I hands the old kingdom to his brother, and the Clyde becomes a Scottish province with its see at Glasgow.
